newsitem.title: UK: Britain a nation of Euro-sceptics - MORI poll.
newsitem.headline: Britain a nation of Euro-sceptics - MORI poll.

text.p: Britain is a nation of Euro-sceptics with a deep mistrust of Europe and considerable resistance to the idea of a European single currency, a MORI poll published on Thursday showed.
The poll, commissioned by ICL Financial Services, shows that 45 percent think the Euro will only be helpful to big business while 59 percent think it would not benefit them personally.
If a single currency were introduced, 51 percent of Britons feel their economy would be controlled from Brussels or Germany and 81 percent feel confused by politicians on the issue.
Asked who they would trust with their money, 73 percent said they would not be confident banking outside Britain while 55 percent would put most trust in a British bank.
Some analysts have predicted that the introduction of a single currency would promote cross-border mergers in the banking and finance sectors.

Following recent tie-ups between banks and retailers, the poll showed that an increasing number of people would open a current account or buy a financial product at a store or other non-traditional supplier.
Of these, Marks & Spencer received the most positive responses with 25 percent followed by British Telecommunications with 21 and Richard Branson's Virgin with 20.
Branson was also the person 62 percent of people would most trust with their money, while Labour Party leader Tony Blair got 24 percent of votes and Prime Minister John Major 21 percent.
British entrepreneur Branson already has a telephone-based financial services company called Virgin Direct which sells insurance and he recently said it was expanding into pensions.
U.K. consumers were favour of a cashless society but only 13 percent expect to use a personal computer or TV for banking services within two years. Only 11 percent use the internet.
